+  <para>All of our imaginary journeys so far have started at the speaker’s location in space and time. Now we are specifying an imaginary journey that starts at a different location, namely at the event of your going to the house. <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section12-example2"/> then says that my going to the market is in the past, relative not to the speaker’s present moment, but instead relative to the moment when you went to the house. <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section12-example2"/> can therefore be translated:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+       I had gone to the market before you went to the house.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>(Other translations are possible, depending on the ever-present context.) Spatial direction and distance sumti tcita are exactly analogous:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example3"/>12.3)  le ratcu cu citka le cirla vi le panka
+       The rat eats the cheese [short distance] the park.
+       The rat eats the cheese near the park.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e12d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example4"/>12.4)  le ratcu cu citka le cirla vi le vu panka
+       The rat eats the cheese [short distance] the [long distance] park
+       The rat eats the cheese near the faraway park.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e12d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example5"/>12.5)  le ratcu cu citka le cirla vu le vi panka
+       The rat eats the cheese [long distance] the [short distance] park
+       The rat eats the cheese far away from the nearby park.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>The event contours of selma'o ZAhO (and their space equivalents, prefixed with “fe'e”) are also useful as sumti tcita. The interpretation of ZAhO tcita differs from that of FAhA, VA, PU, and ZI tcita, however. The event described in the sumti is viewed as a process, and the action of the main bridi occurs at the phase of the process which the ZAhO specifies, or at least some part of that phase. The action of the main bridi itself is seen as a point event, so that there is no issue about which phase of the main bridi is intended. For example:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example6"/>12.6)  mi morsi ba'o le nu mi jmive
+       I am-dead [perfective] the event-of I live.
+       I die in the aftermath of my living.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the (point-)event of my being dead is the portion of my living-process which occurs after the process is complete. Contrast <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section12-example6"/> with:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example7"/>12.7)  mi morsi ba le nu mi jmive
+       I am-dead [future] the event-of I live.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>As explained in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section6"/>, <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section12-example7"/> does not exclude the possibility that I died before I ceased to live!</para>
+  <para>Likewise, we might say:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example8"/>12.8)  mi klama le zarci pu'o le nu mi citka
+       I go-to the store [inchoative] the event-of I eat
+</programlisting>
+  <para>which indicates that before my eating begins, I go to the store, whereas</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example9"/>12.9)  mi klama le zarci ba'o le nu mi citka
+       I go-to the store [perfective] the event-of I eat
+</programlisting>
+  <para>would indicate that I go to the store after I am finished eating.</para>
+  <para>Here is an example which mixes temporal ZAhO (as a tense) and spatial ZAhO (as a sumti tcita):</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d10"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example10"/>12.10) le bloti pu za'o xelklama
+             fe'e ba'o le lalxu
+       The boat [past] [superfective] is-a-transport-mechanism
+             [space] [perfective] the lake.
+       The boat sailed for too long and beyond the lake.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Probably it sailed up onto the dock. One point of clarification: although “xelklama” appears to mean simply “is-a-mode-of-transport”, it does not — the bridi of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section12-example10"/> has four omitted arguments, and thus has the (physical) journey which goes on too long as part of its meaning.</para>
+  <para>The remaining tense cmavo, which have to do with interval size, dimension, and continuousness (or lack thereof) are interpreted to let the sumti specify the particular interval over which the main bridi operates:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d11"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example11"/>12.11) mi klama le zarci reroi le ca djedi
+       I go-to the market [twice] the [present] day.
+       I go/went/will go to the market twice today.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Be careful not to confuse a tense used as a sumti tcita with a tense used within a seltcita sumti:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d12"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example12"/>12.12) loi snime cu carvi ze'u le ca dunra
+       Some-of-the-mass-of snow rains [long time interval] the [present] winter.
+       Snow falls during this winter.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>claims that the interval specified by “this winter” is long, as events of snowfall go, whereas</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e12d13"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section12-example13"/>12.13) loi snime cu carvi ca le ze'u dunra
+       Some-of-the-mass-of snow rains [present] the [long time] winter.
+       Snow falls in the long winter.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>claims that during some part of the winter, which is long as winters go, snow falls.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13">
+  <title>13. Sticky and multiple tenses: KI</title>
+  <para>The following cmavo is discussed in this section:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+     ki      KI                  sticky tense set/reset
+</programlisting>
+  <para>So far we have only considered tenses in isolated bridi. Lojban provides several ways for a tense to continue in effect over more than a single bridi. This property is known as “stickiness”: the tense gets “stuck” and remains in effect until explicitly “unstuck”. In the metaphor of the imaginary journey, the place and time set by a sticky tense may be thought of as a campsite or way-station: it provides a permanent origin with respect to which other tenses are understood. Later imaginary journeys start from that point rather than from the speaker.</para>
+  <para>To make a tense sticky, suffix “ki” to it:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example1"/>13.1)  mi puki klama le zarci .i le nanmu cu batci le gerku
+       I [past] [sticky] go-to the market. The man bites the dog.
+       I went to the market. The man bit the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the use of “puki” rather than just “pu” ensures that the tense will affect the next sentence as well. Otherwise, since the second sentence is tenseless, there would be no way of determining its tense; the event of the second sentence might happen before, after, or simultaneously with that of the first sentence.</para>
+  <para>(The last statement does not apply when the two sentences form part of a narrative. See <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14"/> for an explanation of “story time”, which employs a different set of conventions.)</para>
+  <para>What if the second sentence has a tense anyway?</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example2"/>13.2)  mi puki klama le zarci .i le nanmu pu batci le gerku
+       I [past] [sticky] go-to the market. The man [past] bites the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the second “pu” does not replace the sticky tense, but adds to it, in the sense that the starting point of its imaginary journey is taken to be the previously set sticky time. So the translation of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example2"/> is:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example3"/>13.3)  I went to the market. The man had earlier bitten the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>and it is equivalent in meaning (when considered in isolation from any other sentences) to:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example4"/>13.4)  mi pu klama le zarci .i le nanmu pupu batci le gerku
+       I [past] go-to the market. The man [past] [past] bites the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>The point has not been discussed so far, but it is perfectly grammatical to have more than one tense construct in a sentence:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example5"/>13.5)  puku mi ba klama le zarci
+       [past] I [future] go-to the market.
+       Earlier, I was going to go to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here there are two tenses in the same bridi, the first floating free and specified by “puku”, the second in the usual place and specified by “ba”. They are considered cumulative in the same way as the two tenses in separate sentences of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example4"/>. <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example5"/> is therefore equivalent in meaning, except for emphasis, to:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example6"/>13.6)  mi puba klama le zarci
+       I [past] [future] go-to the market.
+       I was going to go to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Compare <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example7"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example8"/>, which have a different meaning from <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example5"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example6"/>:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example7"/>13.7)  mi ba klama le zarci puku
+       I [future] go-to the market [past].
+       I will have gone to the market earlier.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e13d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example8"/>13.8)  mi bapu klama le zarci
+       I [future] [past] go-to the market.
+       I will have gone to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>So when multiple tense constructs in a single bridi are involved, order counts — the tenses cannot be shifted around as freely as if there were only one tense to worry about.</para>
+  <para>But why bother to allow multiple tense constructs at all? They specify separate portions of the imaginary journey, and can be useful in order to make part of a tense sticky. Consider <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example9"/>, which adds a second bridi and a “ki” to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example5"/>:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example9"/>13.9)  pukiku mi ba klama le zarci .i le nanmu cu batci le gerku
+       [past] [sticky] I [future] go-to the market. The man bites the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>What is the implied tense of the second sentence? Not “puba”, but only “pu”, since only “pu” was made sticky with “ki”. So the translation is:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+       I was going to go to the market. The man bit the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Lojban has several ways of embedding a bridi within another bridi: descriptions, abstractors, relative clauses. (Technically, descriptions contain selbri rather than bridi.) Any of the selbri of these subordinate bridi may have tenses attached. These tenses are interpreted relative to the tense of the main bridi:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d10"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example10"/>13.10) mi pu klama le ba'o zarci
+       I [past] go-to the [perfective] market
+       I went to the former market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>The significance of the “ba'o” in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13-example10"/> is that the speaker’s destination is described as being “in the aftermath of being a market”; that is, it is a market no longer. In particular, the time at which it was no longer a market is in the speaker’s past, because the “ba'o” is interpreted relative to the “pu” tense of the main bridi.</para>
+  <para>Here is an example involving an abstraction bridi:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e13d11"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section13-example11"/>13.11) mi ca jinvi le du'u mi ba morsi
+       I now opine the fact-that I will-be dead.
+       I now believe that I will be dead.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the event of being dead is said to be in the future with respect to the opinion, which is in the present.</para>
+  <para>“ki” may also be used as a tense by itself. This cancels all stickiness and returns the bridi and all following bridi to the speaker’s location in both space and time.</para>
+  <para>In complex descriptions, multiple tenses may be saved and then used by adding a subscript to “ki”. A time made sticky with “kixipa” (ki-sub-1) can be returned to by specifying “kixipa” as a tense by itself. In the case of written expression, the writer’s here-and-now is often different from the reader’s, and a pair of subscripted “ki” tenses could be used to distinguish the two.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14">
+  <title>14. Story time</title>
+  <para>Making strict use of the conventions explained in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13"/> would be intolerably awkward when a story is being told. The time at which a story is told by the narrator is usually unimportant to the story. What matters is the flow of time within the story itself. The term “story” in this section refers to any series of statements related in more-or-less time-sequential order, not just a fictional one.</para>
+  <para>Lojban speakers use a different set of conventions, commonly called “story time”, for inferring tense within a story. It is presumed that the event described by each sentence takes place some time more or less after the previous ones. Therefore, tenseless sentences are implicitly tensed as “what happens next”. In particular, any sticky time setting is advanced by each sentence.</para>
+  <para>The following mini-story illustrates the important features of story time. A sentence-by-sentence explication follows:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e14d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example1"/>14.1)  puzuki ku ne'iki le kevna
+             le ninmu goi ko'a zutse le rokci
+       [past] [long] [sticky] [,] [inside] [sticky] the cave,
+             the woman defined-as she-1 sat-on the rock
+       Long ago, in a cave, a woman sat on a rock.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e14d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example2"/>14.2)  .i ko'a citka loi kanba rectu
+       She-1 [tenseless] eat some-of-the-mass-of goat flesh.
+       She was eating goat’s meat.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e14d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example3"/>14.3)  .i ko'a pu jukpa ri le mudyfagri
+       She [past] cook the-last-mentioned by-method the wood-fire.
+       She had cooked the meat over a wood fire.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e14d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example4"/>14.4)  .i lei rectu cu zanglare
+       The-mass-of flesh is-(favorable)-warm.
+       The meat was pleasantly warm.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e14d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example5"/>14.5)  .i le labno goi ko'e bazaki nenri klama le kevna
+       The wolf defined-as it-2 [future] [medium] [sticky] within-came to-the cave.
+       A while later, a wolf came into the cave.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e14d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example6"/>14.6)  .i ko'e lebna lei rectu ko'a
+       It-2 [tenseless] takes the-mass-of flesh from-her-1.
+       It took the meat from her.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e14d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section14-example7"/>14.7)  .i ko'e bartu klama
+       It-2 out ran
+       It ran out.
+</programlisting>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example1"/> sets both the time (long ago) and the place (in a cave) using “ki”, just like the sentence sequences in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13"/>. No further space cmavo are used in the rest of the story, so the place is assumed to remain unchanged. The English translation of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example1"/> is marked for past tense also, as the conventions of English storytelling require: consequently, all other English translation sentences are also in the past tense. (We don’t notice how strange this is; even stories about the future are written in past tense!) This conventional use of past tense is not used in Lojban narratives.</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example2"/> is tenseless. Outside story time, it would be assumed that its event happens simultaneously with that of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example1"/>, since a sticky tense is in effect; the rules of story time, however, imply that the event occurs afterwards, and that the story time has advanced (changing the sticky time set in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example1"/>).</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example3"/> has an explicit tense. This is taken relative to the latest setting of the sticky time; therefore, the event of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example3"/> happens before that of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example2"/>. It cannot be determined if <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example3"/> happens before or after <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example1"/>.</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example4"/> is again tenseless. Story time was not changed by the flashback in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example3"/>, so <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example4"/> happens after <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example2"/>.</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example5"/> specifies the future (relative to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example4"/>) and makes it sticky. So all further events happen after <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example5"/>.</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example6"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example7"/> are again tenseless, and so happen after <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section14-example5"/>. (Story time is changed.)</para>
+  <para>So the overall order is 14.1 - 14.3 - 14.2 - 14.4 - (medium interval) - 14.5 - 14.6 - 14.7. It is also possible that 14.3 happens before 14.1.</para>
+  <para>If no sticky time (or space) is set initially, the story is set at an unspecified time (or space): the effect is like that of choosing an arbitrary reference point and making it sticky. This style is common in stories that are jokes. The same convention may be used if the context specifies the sticky time sufficiently.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15">
+  <title>15. Tenses in subordinate bridi</title>
+  <para>English has a set of rules, formally known as “sequence of tense rules”, for determining what tense should be used in a subordinate clause, depending on the tense used in the main sentence. Here are some examples:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e15d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example1"/>15.1)  John says that George is going to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e15d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example2"/>15.2)  John says that George went to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e15d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example3"/>15.3)  John said that George went to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e15d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example4"/>15.4)  John said that George had gone to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>In <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example1"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example2"/>, the tense of the main sentence is the present: “says”. If George goes when John speaks, we get the present tense “is going” (“goes” would be unidiomatic); if George goes before John speaks, we get the past tense “went”. But if the tense of the main sentence is the past, with “said”, then the tense required in the subordinate clause is different. If George goes when John speaks, we get the past tense “went”; if George goes before John speaks, we get the past-perfect tense “had gone”.</para>
+  <para>The rule of English, therefore, is that both the tense of the main sentence and the tense of the subordinate clause are understood relative to the speaker of the main sentence (not John, but the person who speaks <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example1"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example4"/>).</para>
+  <para>Lojban, like Russian and Esperanto, uses a different convention. A tense in a subordinate bridi is understood to be relative to the tense already set in the main bridi. Thus <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example1"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example4"/> can be expressed in Lojban respectively thus:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e15d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example5"/>15.5)  la djan. ca cusku le se du'u la djordj. ca klama le zarci
+       John [present] says the statement-that George [present] goes-to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e15d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example6"/>15.6)  la djan. ca cusku le se du'u la djordj. pu klama le zarci
+       John [present] says the statement-that George [past] goes-to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e15d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example7"/>15.7)  la djan. pu cusku le se du'u la djordj. ca klama le zarci
+       John [past] says the statement-that George [present] goes-to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e15d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example8"/>15.8)  la djan. pu cusku le se du'u la djordj. pu klama le zarci
+       John [past] says the statement-that George [past] goes-to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Probably the most counterintuitive of the Lojban examples is <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section15-example7"/>. The “ca” looks quite odd, as if George were going to the market right now, rather than back when John spoke. But this “ca” is really a “ca” with respect to a reference point specified by the outer “pu”. This behavior is the same as the additive behavior of multiple tenses in the same bridi, as explained in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section13"/>.</para>
+  <para>There is a special cmavo “nau” (of selma'o CUhE) which can be used to override these rules and get to the speaker’s current reference point. (Yes, it sounds like English “now”.) It is not grammatical to combine “nau” with any other cmavo in a tense, except by way of a logical or non-logical connection (see <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section20"/>). Here is a convoluted sentence with several nested bridi which uses “nau” at the lowest level:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e15d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section15-example9"/>15.9)  la djan. pu cusku le se du'u la .alis pu cusku le se du'u
+                 la djordj. pu cusku le se du'u la maris. nau klama le zarci
+       John [past] says the statement-that Alice [past] says the statement-that
+                 George [past] says the statement that Mary [now] goes-to the market.
+       John said that Alice had said that George had earlier said that Mary is now going to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>The use of “nau” does not affect sticky tenses.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16">
+  <title>16. Tense relations between sentences</title>
+  <para>The sumti tcita method, explained in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section12"/>, of asserting a tense relationship between two events suffers from asymmetry. Specifically,</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example1"/>16.1)  le verba cu cadzu le bisli zu'a le nu le nanmu cu batci le gerku
+       The child walks-on the ice [left] the event-of the man bites the dog.
+       The child walks on the ice to the left of where the man bites the dog.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>which specifies an imaginary journey leftward from the man biting the dog to the child walking on the ice, claims only that the child walks on the ice. By the nature of “le nu”, the man’s biting the dog is merely referred to without being claimed. If it seems desirable to claim both, each event can be expressed as a main sentence bridi, with a special form of “.i” connecting them:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/>16.2)  le nanmu cu batci le gerku .izu'abo le verba cu cadzu le bisli
+       The man bites the dog. [Left] the child walks-on the ice.
+       The man bites the dog. To the left, the child walks on the ice.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>“.izu'abo” is a compound cmavo: the “.i” separates the sentences and the “zu'a” is the tense. The “bo” is required to prevent the “zu'a” from gobbling up the following sumti, namely “le verba”.</para>
+  <para>Note that the bridi in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/> appear in the reverse order from their appearance in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example1"/>. With “.izu'abo” (and all other afterthought tense connectives) the sentence specifying the origin of the journey comes first. This is a natural order for sentences, but requires some care when converting between this form and the sumti tcita form.</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/> means the same thing as:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example3"/>16.3)  le nanmu cu batci le gerku
+             .i zu'a la'edi'u le verba cu cadzu le bisli
+       The man bites the dog.
+             [Left] the-referent-of-the-last-sentence the child walks-on the ice.
+       The man bites the dog. Left of what I just mentioned, the child walks on the ice.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>If the “bo” is omitted in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/>, the meaning changes:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example4"/>16.4)  le nanmu cu batci le gerku .i zu'a le verba cu cadzu le bisli
+       The man bites the dog. [Left] the child [something] walks-on the ice.
+       The man bites the dog. To the left of the child, something walks on the ice.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the first place of the second sentence is unspecified, because “zu'a” has absorbed the sumti “le verba”.</para>
+  <para>Do not confuse either <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/> or <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example4"/> with the following:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example5"/>16.5)  le nanmu cu batci le gerku .i zu'aku le verba cu cadzu le bisli
+       The man bites the dog. [Left] the child walks-on the ice.
+       The man bites the dog. Left of me, the child walks on the ice.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>In <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example5"/>, the origin point is the speaker, as is usual with “zu'aku”. <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/> makes the origin point of the tense the event described by the first sentence.</para>
+  <para>Two sentences may also be connected in forethought by a tense relationship. Just like afterthought tense connection, forethought tense connection claims both sentences, and in addition claims that the time or space relationship specified by the tense holds between the events the two sentences describe.</para>
+  <para>The origin sentence is placed first, preceded by a tense plus “gi”. Another “gi” is used to separate the sentences:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example6"/>16.6)  pugi mi klama le zarci gi mi klama le zdani
+       [past] I go-to the market [,] I go-to the house.
+       Before I go to the market, I go to the house.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>A parallel construction can be used to express a tense relationship between sumti:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example7"/>16.7)  mi klama pugi le zarci gi le zdani
+       I go-to [past] the market [,] the house.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Because English does not have any direct way of expressing a tense-like relationship between nouns, <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example7"/> cannot be expressed in English without paraphrasing it either into <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example6"/> or else into “I go to the house before the market”, which is ambiguous — is the market going?</para>
+  <para>Finally, a third forethought construction expresses a tense relationship between bridi-tails rather than whole bridi. (The construct known as a “bridi-tail” is explained fully in <xref linkend="cll_chapter14"/>; roughly speaking, it is a selbri, possibly with following sumti.) <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example8"/> is equivalent in meaning to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example6"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example7"/>:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e16d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section16-example8"/>16.8)  mi pugi klama le zarci gi klama le zdani
+       I [past] go-to the market [,] go-to the house.
+       I, before going to the market, go to the house.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>In both <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example7"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example8"/>, the underlying sentences “mi klama le zarci” and “mi klama le zdani” are not claimed; only the relationship in time between them is claimed.</para>
+  <para>Both the forethought and the afterthought forms are appropriate with PU, ZI, FAhA, VA, and ZAhO tenses. In all cases, the equivalent forms are (where X and Y stand for sentences, and TENSE for a tense cmavo):</para>
+  <programlisting>
+      subordinate:               X TENSE le nu Y
+      afterthought coordinate:   Y .i+TENSE+bo X
+      forethought coordinate:    TENSE+gi X gi Y
+</programlisting>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17">
+  <title>17. Tensed logical connectives</title>
+  <para>The Lojban tense system interacts with the Lojban logical connective system. That system is a separate topic, explained in <xref linkend="cll_chapter14"/> and touched on only in summary here. By the rules of the logical connective system, <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example1"/> through 17.3 are equivalent in meaning:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e17d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example1"/>17.1)  la teris. satre le mlatu .ije la teris. satre le ractu
+       Terry strokes the cat. And Terry strokes the rabbit.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example2"/>17.2)  la teris. satre le mlatu gi'e satre le ractu
+       Terry strokes the cat and strokes the rabbit.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example3"/>17.3)  la teris. satre le mlatu .e le ractu
+       Terry strokes the cat and the rabbit.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Suppose we wish to add a tense relationship to the logical connective “and”? To say that Terry strokes the cat and later strokes the rabbit, we can combine a logical connective with a tense connective by placing the logical connective first, then the tense, and then the cmavo “bo”, thus:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e17d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example4"/>17.4)  la teris. satre le mlatu .ijebabo la teris. satre le ractu
+       Terry strokes the cat. And then Terry strokes the rabbit.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example5"/>17.5)  la teris. satre le mlatu gi'ebabo satre le ractu
+       Terry strokes the cat, and then strokes the rabbit.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example6"/>17.6)  la teris. satre le mlatu .ebabo le ractu
+       Terry strokes the cat and then the rabbit.
+</programlisting>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example4"/> through 17.6 are equivalent in meaning. They are also analogous to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example1"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example3"/> respectively. The “bo” is required for the same reason as in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section16-example2"/>: to prevent the “ba” from functioning as a sumti tcita for the following sumti (or, in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example5"/>, from being attached to the following selbri).</para>
+  <para>In addition to the “bo” construction of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example4"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example6"/>, there is also a form of tensed logical connective with “ke ... ke'e” (“tu'e ... tu'u” for sentences). The logical connective system makes <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example7"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example9"/> equivalent in meaning:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e17d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example7"/>17.7)  mi bevri le dakli .ije tu'e mi bevri le gerku .ija mi bevri le mlatu tu'u
+       I carry the sack. And (I carry the dog. And/or I carry the cat).
+       I carry the sack. And I carry the dog, or I carry the cat, or I carry both.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example8"/>17.8)  mi bevri le dakli gi'eke bevri le gerku gi'a bevri le mlatu
+       I carry the sack and (carry the dog and/or carry the cat).
+       I carry the sack, and also carry the dog or carry the cat or carry both.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example9"/>17.9)  mi bevri le dakli .eke le gerku .a le mlatu
+       I carry the sack and (the dog or the cat).
+       I carry the sack and also the dog or the cat or both.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Note the uniformity of the Lojban, as contrasted with the variety of ways in which the English provides for the correct grouping. In all cases, the meaning is that I carry the sack in any case, and either the cat or the dog or both.</para>
+  <para>To express that I carry the sack first (earlier in time), and then the dog or the cat or both simultaneously, I can insert tenses to form <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example10"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example12"/>:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e17d10"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example10"/>17.10) mi bevri le dakli .ije ba tu'e mi bevri le gerku
+            .ijacabo mi bevri le mlatu tu'u
+       I carry the sack.  And [future] (I carry the dog.
+            And/or [present] I carry the cat.)
+       I carry the sack. And then I will carry the dog or I will carry the cat
+            or I will carry both at once.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d11"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example11"/>17.11) mi bevri le dakli gi'ebake bevri le gerku gi'acabo bevri le mlatu
+       I carry the sack and [future] (carry the dog and/or [present] carry the cat).
+       I carry the sack and then will carry the dog or carry the cat or carry both at once.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e17d12"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section17-example12"/>17.12) mi bevri le dakli .ebake le gerku .acabo le mlatu
+       I carry the sack and [future] (the cat and/or [present] the dog).
+       I carry the sack, and then the cat or the dog or both at once.
+</programlisting>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example10"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example12"/> are equivalent in meaning to each other, and correspond to the tenseless <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example7"/> through <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section17-example9"/> respectively.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18">
+  <title>18. Tense negation</title>
+  <para>Any bridi which involves tenses of selma'o PU, FAhA, or ZAhO can be contradicted by a “-nai” suffixed to the tense cmavo. Some examples:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e18d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example1"/>18.1)  mi punai klama le zarci
+       I [past] [not] go-to the market.
+       I didn’t go to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>As a contradictory negation, <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section18-example1"/> implies that the bridi as a whole is false without saying anything about what is true. When the negated tense is a sumti tcita, “-nai” negation indicates that the stated relationship does not hold:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e18d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example2"/>18.2)  mi klama le zarci canai le nu do klama le zdani
+       I go-to the market [present] [not] the event-of you go-to the house.
+       It is not true that I went to the market at the same time that you went to the house.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e18d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example3"/>18.3)  le nanmu batci le gerku ne'inai le kumfa
+       The man bites the dog [within] [not] the room.
+       The man didn’t bite the dog inside the room.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e18d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example4"/>18.4)  mi morsi ca'onai le nu mi jmive
+       I am-dead [continuitive - negated] the event-of I live.
+       It is false that I am dead during my life.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>It is also possible to perform scalar negation of whole tense constructs by placing a member of NAhE before them. Unlike contradictory negation, scalar negation asserts a truth: that the bridi is true with some tense other than that specified. The following examples are scalar negation analogues of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section18-example1"/> to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section18-example3"/>:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e18d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example5"/>18.5)  mi na'e pu klama le zarci
+       I [non-] [past] go-to the market.
+       I go to the market other than in the past.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e18d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example6"/>18.6)  le nanmu batci le gerku to'e ne'i le kumfa
+       The man bites the dog [opposite-of] [within] the room.
+       The man bites the dog outside the room.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e18d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example7"/>18.7)  mi klama le zarci na'e ca le nu do klama le zdani
+       I go-to the market [non-] [present] the event-of you go-to the house.
+       I went to the market at a time other than the time at which you went to the house.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e18d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example8"/>18.8)  mi morsi na'e ca'o le nu mi jmive
+       I am-dead [non-] [continuitive] the event-of I live.
+       I am dead other than during my life.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Unlike “-nai” contradictory negation, scalar negation of tenses is not limited to PU and FAhA:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e18d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section18-example9"/>18.9)  le verba na'e ri'u cadzu le bisli
+       The child [non-] [right] walks-on the ice
+       The child walks on the ice other than to my right.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>The use of “-nai” on cmavo of TAhE and ROI has already been discussed in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section9"/>; this use is also a scalar negation.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19">
+  <title>19. Actuality, potentiality, capability: CAhA</title>
+  <para>The following cmavo are discussed in this section:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+     ca'a    CAhA                actually is
+     ka'e    CAhA                is innately capable of
+     nu'o    CAhA                can but has not
+     pu'i    CAhA                can and has
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Lojban bridi without tense markers may not necessarily refer to actual events: they may also refer to capabilities or potential events. For example:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example1"/>19.1)  ro datka cu flulimna
+       All ducks are-float-swimmers.
+       All ducks swim by floating.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>is a Lojban truth, even though the colloquial English translation is false or at best ambiguous. This is because the tenseless Lojban bridi doesn’t necessarily claim that every duck is swimming or floating now or even at a specific time or place. Even if we add a tense marker to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section19-example1"/>,</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example2"/>19.2)  ro datka ca flulimna
+       All ducks [present] are-float-swimmers.
+       All ducks are now swimming by floating.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>the resulting <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section19-example2"/> might still be considered a truth, even though the colloquial English seems even more likely to be false. All ducks have the potential of swimming even if they are not exercising that potential at present. To get the full flavor of “All ducks are now swimming”, we must append a marker from selma'o CAhA to the tense, and say:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example3"/>19.3)  ro datka ca ca'a flulimna
+       All ducks [present] [actual] are-float-swimmers.
+       All ducks are now actually swimming by floating.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>A CAhA cmavo is always placed after any other tense cmavo, whether for time or for space. However, a CAhA cmavo comes before “ki”, so that a CAhA condition can be made sticky.</para>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section19-example3"/> is false in both Lojban and English, since it claims that the swimming is an actual, present fact, true of every duck that exists, whereas in fact there is at least one duck that is not swimming now.</para>
+  <para>Furthermore, some ducks are dead (and therefore sink); some ducks have just hatched (and do not know how to swim yet), and some ducks have been eaten by predators (and have ceased to exist as separate objects at all). Nevertheless, all these ducks have the innate capability of swimming — it is part of the nature of duckhood. The cmavo “ka'e” expresses this notion of innate capability:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example4"/>19.4)  ro datka ka'e flulimna
+       All ducks [capable] are-float-swimmers.
+       All ducks are innately capable of swimming.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Under some epistemologies, innate capability can be extended in order to apply the innate properties of a mass to which certain individuals belong to the individuals themselves, even if those individuals are themselves not capable of fulfilling the claim of the bridi. For example:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example5"/>19.5)  la djan. ka'e viska
+       John [capable] sees.
+       John is innately capable of seeing.
+       John can see.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>might be true about a human being named John, even though he has been blind since birth, because the ability to see is innately built into his nature as a human being. It is theoretically possible that conditions might occur that would enable John to see (a great medical discovery, for example). On the other hand,</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example6"/>19.6)  le cukta ka'e viska
+       The book [capable] sees.
+       The book can see.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>is not true in most epistemologies, since the ability to see is not part of the innate nature of a book.</para>
+  <para>Consider once again the newly hatched ducks mentioned earlier. They have the potential of swimming, but have not yet demonstrated that potential. This may be expressed using “nu'o”, the cmavo of CAhA for undemonstrated potential:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example7"/>19.7)  ro cifydatka nu'o flulimna
+       All infant-ducks [can but has not] are-float-swimmers.
+       All infant ducks have an undemonstrated potential for swimming by floating.
+       Baby ducks can swim but haven’t yet.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Contrariwise, if Frank is not blind from birth, then “pu'i” is appropriate:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example8"/>19.8)  la frank. pu'i viska
+       Frank [can and has] sees.
+       Frank has demonstrated a potential for seeing.
+       Frank can see and has seen.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Note that the glosses given at the beginning of this section for “ca'a”, “nu'o”, and “pu'i” incorporate “ca” into their meaning, and are really correct for “ca ca'a”, “ca nu'o”, and “ca pu'i”. However, the CAhA cmavo are perfectly meaningful with other tenses than the present:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example9"/>19.9)  mi pu ca'a klama le zarci
+       I [past] [actual] go-to the store.
+       I actually went to the store.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e19d10"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example10"/>19.10) la frank. ba nu'o klama le zdani
+       Frank [future] [can but has not] goes-to the store.
+       Frank could have, but will not have, gone to the store
+            (at some understood moment in the future).
+</programlisting>
+  <para>As always in Lojban tenses, a missing CAhA can have an indeterminate meaning, or the context can be enough to disambiguate it. Saying</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d11"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example11"/>19.11) ta jelca
+       That burns/is-burning/might-burn/will-burn.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>with no CAhA specified can translate the two very different English sentences “That is on fire” and “That is inflammable.” The first demands immediate action (usually), whereas the second merely demands caution. The two cases can be disambiguated with:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d12"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example12"/>19.12) ta ca ca'a jelca
+       That [present] [actual] burns.
+       That is on fire.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>and</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d13"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example13"/>19.13) ta ka'e jelca
+       That [capable] burns.
+       That is capable of burning.
+       That is inflammable.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>When no indication is given, as in the simple observative</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e19d14"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section19-example14"/>19.14) jelca
+       It burns!
+</programlisting>
+  <para>the prudent Lojbanist will assume the meaning “Fire!”</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20">
+  <title>20. Logical and non-logical connections between tenses</title>
+  <para>Like many things in Lojban, tenses may be logically connected; logical connection is explained in more detail in <xref linkend="cll_chapter14"/>. Some of the terminology in this section will be clear only if you already understand logical connectives.</para>
+  <para>The appropriate logical connectives belong to selma'o JA. A logical connective between tenses can always be expanded to one between sentences:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e20d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example1"/>20.1)  mi pu je ba klama le zarci
+       I [past] and [future] go-to the market.
+       I went and will go to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>means the same as:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e20d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example2"/>20.2)  mi pu klama le zarci .ije mi ba klama le zarci
+       I [past] go-to the market. And I [future] go-to the market.
+       I went to the market, and I will go to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Tense connection and tense negation are combined in:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e20d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example3"/>20.3)  mi punai je canai je ba klama le zarci
+       I [past] [not] and [present] [not] and [future] go-to the market.
+       I haven’t yet gone to the market, but I will in future.
+</programlisting>
+  <para><xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section20-example3"/> is far more specific than</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e20d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example4"/>20.4)  mi ba klama le zarci
+       I [future] go-to the market.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>which only says that I will go, without claiming anything about my past or present. “ba” does not imply “punai” or “canai”; to compel that interpretation, either a logical connection or a ZAhO is needed.</para>
+  <para>Tense negation can often be removed in favor of negation in the logical connective itself. The following examples are equivalent in meaning:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e20d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example5"/>20.5)  mi mo'izu'anai je mo'iri'u cadzu
+       I [motion] [left-not] and [motion] [right] walk.
+       I walk not leftward but rightward.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e20d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example6"/>20.6)  mi mo'izu'a naje mo'iri'u cadzu
+       I [motion] [left] not-and [motion] [right] walk.
+       I walk not leftward but rightward.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>There are no forethought logical connections between tenses allowed by the grammar, to keep tenses simpler. Nor is there any way to override simple left-grouping of the connectives, the Lojban default.</para>
+  <para>The non-logical connectives of selma'o JOI, BIhI, and GAhO are also permitted between tenses. One application is to specify intervals not by size, but by their end-points (“bi'o” belongs to selma'o BIhI, and connects the end-points of an ordered interval, like English “from ... to”):</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e20d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section20-example7"/>20.7)  mi puza bi'o bazu vasxu
+       I [past] [medium] from ... to [future] [long] breathe.
+       I breathe from a medium time ago till a long time to come.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>(It is to be hoped that I have a long life ahead of me.)</para>
+  <para>One additional use of non-logical connectives within tenses is discussed in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section21"/>. Other uses will probably be identified in future.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section21">
+  <title>21. Sub-events</title>
+  <para>Another application of non-logical tense connection is to talk about sub-events of events. Consider a six-shooter: a gun which can fire six bullets in succession before reloading. If I fire off the entire magazine twice, I can express the fact in Lojban thus:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e21d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section21-example1"/>21.1)  mi reroi pi'u xaroi cecla le seldanti
+       I [twice] [cross-product] [six times] shoot the projectile-launcher.
+       On two occasions, I fire the gun six times.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>It would be confusing, though grammatical, to run the “reroi” and the “xaroi” directly together. However, the non-logical connective “pi'u” expresses a Cartesian product (also known as a cross product) of two sets. In this case, there is a set of two firings each of which is represented by a set of six shots, for twelve shots in all (hence the name “product”: the product of 2 and 6 is 12). Its use specifies very precisely what occurs.</para>
+  <para>In fact, you can specify strings of interval properties and event contours within a single tense without the use of a logical or non-logical connective cmavo. This allows tenses of the type:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e21d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section21-example2"/>21.2)  la djordj. ca'o co'a ciska
+       George [continuitive] [initiative] writes.
+       George continues to start to write.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e21d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section21-example3"/>21.3)  mi reroi ca'o xaroi darxi le damri
+       I [twice] [continuitive] [six times] hit the drum.
+       On two occasions, I continue to beat the drum six times.
+</programlisting>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22">
+  <title>22. Conversion of sumti tcita: JAI</title>
+  <para>The following cmavo are discussed in this section:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+     jai     JAI                 tense conversion
+     fai     FA                  indefinite place
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Conversion is the regular Lojban process of moving around the places of a place structure. The cmavo of selma'o SE serve this purpose, exchanging the first place with one of the others:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example1"/>22.1)  mi cu klama le zarci
+       I go-to the market.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e22d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example2"/>22.2)  le zarci cu se klama mi
+       The market is-gone-to by-me.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>It is also possible to bring a place that is specified by a sumti tcita (for the purposes of this chapter, a tense sumti tcita) to the front, by using “jai” plus the tense as the grammatical equivalent of SE:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example3"/>22.3)  le ratcu cu citka le cirla vi le panka
+       The rat eats the cheese [short distance] the park.
+       The rat eats the cheese in the park.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e22d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example4"/>22.4)  le panka cu jai vi citka le cirla fai le ratcu
+       The park is-the-place-of eating the cheese by-the rat.
+       The park is where the rat eats the cheese.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>In <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section22-example4"/>, the construction JAI+tense converts the location sumti into the first place. The previous first place has nowhere to go, since the location sumti is not a numbered place; however, it can be inserted back into the bridi with “fai”, the indefinite member of selma'o FA.</para>
+  <para>(The other members of FA are used to mark the first, second, etc. places of a bridi explicitly:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example5"/>22.5)  fa mi cu klama fe le zarci
+</programlisting>
+  <para>means the same as</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example6"/>22.6)  fe le zarci cu klama fa mi
+</programlisting>
+  <para>as well as the simple</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example7"/>22.7)  mi cu klama le zarci
+</programlisting>
+  <para>in which the place structure is determined by position.)</para>
+  <para>Like SE conversion, JAI+tense conversion is especially useful in descriptions with LE selma'o:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example8"/>22.8)  mi viska le jai vi citka be le cirla
+       I saw the place-of eating the cheese.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the eater of the cheese is elided, so no “fai” appears.</para>
+  <para>Of course, temporal tenses are also usable with JAI:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e22d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section22-example9"/>22.9)  mi djuno fi le jai ca morsi be fai la djan.
+       I know about the [present] is-dead of-the-one-called “John”.
+       I know the time of John’s death.
+       I know when John died.
+</programlisting>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23">
+  <title>23. Tenses versus modals</title>
+  <para>Grammatically, every use of tenses seen so far is exactly paralleled by some use of modals as explained in <xref linkend="cll_chapter9"/>. Modals and tenses alike can be followed by sumti, can appear before the selbri, can be used in pure and mixed connections, can participate in JAI conversions. The parallelism is perfect. However, there is a deep difference in the semantics of tense constructs and modal constructs, grounded in historical differences between the two forms. Originally, modals and tenses were utterly different things in earlier versions of Loglan; only in Lojban have they become grammatically interchangeable. And even now, differences in semantics continue to be maintained.</para>
+  <para>The core distinction is that whereas the modal bridi</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example1"/>23.1)  mi nelci do mu'i le nu do nelci mi
+       I like you with-motivation the event-of you like me.
+       I like you because you like me.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>places the “le nu” sumti in the x1 place of the gismu “mukti” (which underlies the modal “mu'i”), namely the motivating event, the tensed bridi</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example2"/>23.2)  mi nelci do ba le nu do nelci mi
+       I like you after the event-of you like me.
+       I like you after you like me.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>places the “le nu” sumti in the x2 place of the gismu “balvi” (which underlies the tense “ba”), namely the point of reference for the future tense. Paraphrases of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example1"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example2"/>, employing the brivla “mukti” and “balvi” explicitly, would be:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example3"/>23.3)  le nu do nelci mi cu mukti le nu mi nelci do
+       The event-of you like me motivates the event-of I like you.
+       Your liking me is the motive for my liking you.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>and</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example4"/>23.4)  le nu mi nelci do cu balvi le nu do nelci mi
+       The event-of I like you is after the event of you like me.
+       My liking you follows (in time) your liking me.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>(Note that the paraphrase is not perfect due to the difference in what is claimed; <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example3"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example4"/> claim only the causal and temporal relationships between the events, not the existence of the events themselves.)</para>
+  <para>As a result, the afterthought sentence-connective forms of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example1"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example2"/> are, respectively:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example5"/>23.5)  mi nelci do .imu'ibo do nelci mi
+       I like you. [That is] Because you like me.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e23d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example6"/>23.6)  do nelci mi .ibabo mi nelci do
+       You like me. Afterward, I like you.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>In <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example5"/>, the order of the two bridi “mi nelci do” and “do nelci mi” is the same as in <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example1"/>. In <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example6"/>, however, the order is reversed: the origin point “do nelci mi” physically appears before the future-time event “mi nelci do”. In both cases, the bridi characterizing the event in the x2 place appears before the bridi characterizing the event in the x1 place of “mukti” or “balvi”.</para>
+  <para>In forethought connections, however, the asymmetry between modals and tenses is not found. The forethought equivalents of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example5"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section23-example6"/> are</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example7"/>23.7)  mu'igi do nelci mi gi mi nelci do
+       Because you like me, I like you.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>and</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e23d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section23-example8"/>23.8)  bagi do nelci mi gi mi nelci do
+       After you like me, I like you.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>respectively.</para>
+  <para>The following modal sentence schemata (where X and Y represent sentences) all have the same meaning:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+       X .i BAI bo Y
+       BAI gi Y gi X
+       X BAI le nu Y
+</programlisting>
+  <para>whereas the following tensed sentence schemata also have the same meaning:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+       X .i TENSE bo Y
+       TENSE gi X gi Y
+       Y TENSE le nu X
+</programlisting>
+  <para>neglecting the question of what is claimed. In the modal sentence schemata, the modal tag is always followed by Y, the sentence representing the event in the x1 place of the gismu that underlies the BAI. In the tensed sentences, no such simple rule exists.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24">
+  <title>24. Tense questions: “cu'e”</title>
+  <para>The following cmavo is discussed in this section:</para>
+  <programlisting>
+     cu'e    CUhE                tense question
+</programlisting>
+  <para>There are two main ways to ask questions about tense. The main English tense question words are “When?” and “Where?”. These may be paraphrased respectively as “At what time?” and “At what place?” In these forms, their Lojban equivalents simply involve a tense plus “ma”, the Lojban sumti question:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e24d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example1"/>24.1)  do klama le zdani ca ma
+       You go-to the house [present] [what sumti?].
+       You go to the house at what time?
+       When do you go to the house?
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e24d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example2"/>24.2)  le verba vi ma pu cadzu le bisli
+       The child [short space] [what sumti?] [past] walks-on the ice.
+       The child at/near what place walked on the ice?
+       Where did the child walk on the ice?
+</programlisting>
+  <para>There is also a non-specific tense and modal question, “cu'e”, belonging to selma'o CUhE. This can be used wherever a tense or modal construct can be used.</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e24d3"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example3"/>24.3)  le nanmu cu'e batci le gerku
+       The man [what tense?] bites the dog.
+       When/Where/How does the man bite the dog?
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Possible answers to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section24-example3"/> might be:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e24d4"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example4"/>24.4)  va
+       [medium space].
+       Some ways from here.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e24d5"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example5"/>24.5)  puzu
+       [past] [long time].
+       A long time ago.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e24d6"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example6"/>24.6)  vi le lunra
+       [short space] The moon.
+       On the moon.
+
+<anchor xml:id="c10e24d7"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example7"/>24.7)  pu'o
+       [inchoative]
+       He hasn’t yet done so.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>or even the modal reply (from selma'o BAI; see <xref linkend="cll_chapter9"/>):</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e24d8"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example8"/>24.8)  seka'a le briju
+       With-destination the office.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>The only way to combine “cu'e” with other tense cmavo is through logical connection, which makes a question that pre-specifies some information:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e24d9"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example9"/>24.9)  do puzi je cu'e sombo le gurni
+       You [past] [short] and [when?] sow the grain?
+       You sowed the grain a little while ago; when else do you sow it?
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Additionally, the logical connective itself can be replaced by a question word:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e24d10"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section24-example10"/>24.10) la .artr. pu je'i ba nolraitru
+       Arthur [past] [which?] [future] is-a-king
+       Was Arthur a king or will he be?
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Answers to <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section24-example10"/> would be logical connectives such as “je”, meaning “both”, “naje” meaning “the latter”, or “jenai” meaning “the former”.</para>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section25">
+  <title>25. Explicit magnitudes</title>
+  <para>It is a limitation of the VA and ZI system of specifying magnitudes that they can only prescribe vague magnitudes: small, medium, or large. In order to express both an origin point and an exact distance, the Lojban construction called a “termset” is employed. (Termsets are explained further in <xref linkend="cll_chapter14"/> and <xref linkend="cll_chapter16"/>.) It is grammatical for a termset to be placed after a tense or modal tag rather than a sumti, which allows both the origin of the imaginary journey and its distance to be specified. Here is an example:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e25d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section25-example1"/>25.1)  la frank. sanli zu'a nu'i la djordj.
+             la'u lo mitre be li mu [nu'u]
+         Frank stands [left] [start termset] George
+             [quantity] a thing-measuring-in-meters the-number 5 [end termset].
+       Frank is standing five meters to the left of George.
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Here the termset extends from the “nu'i” to the implicit “nu'u” at the end of the sentence, and includes the terms “la djordj.”, which is the unmarked origin point, and the tagged sumti “lo mitre be li mu”, which the cmavo “la'u” (of selma'o BAI, and meaning “with quantity”; see <xref linkend="cll_chapter9"/>) marks as a quantity. Both terms are governed by the tag “zu'a”</para>
+  <para>It is not necessary to have both an origin point and an explicit magnitude: a termset may have only a single term in it. A less precise version of <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section25-example1"/> is:</para>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e25d2"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section25-example2"/>25.2)  la frank. sanli zu'a nu'i la'u
+             lo mitre be li mu
+       Frank stands [left] [termset] [quantity]
+             a thing-measuring-in-meters the-number 5.
+       Frank stands five meters to the left.
+</programlisting>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section26">
+  <title>26. Finally (an exercise for the much-tried reader)</title>
+  <programlisting><anchor xml:id="c10e26d1"/><anchor xml:id="cll_chapter10-section26-example1"/>26.1)  .a'o do pu seju ba roroi ca'o fe'e su'oroi jimpe
+            fi le lojbo temci selsku ciste
+</programlisting>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section27">
+  <title>27. Summary of tense selma'o</title>
+  <programlisting>
+      PU    temporal direction
+            pu = past, ca = present, ba = future
+
+      ZI    temporal distance
+            zi = short, za = medium, zu = long
+
+      ZEhA  temporal interval
+            ze'i = short, ze'a = medium, ze'u = long, ze'e = infinite
+
+      ROI   objective quantified tense flag
+            noroi = never, paroi = once, ..., roroi = always, etc.
+            pare'u = the first time, rere'u = the second time, etc.
+
+      TAhE  subjective quantified tense
+            di'i = regularly, na'o = typically, ru'i = continuously, ta'e = habitually
+
+      ZAhO  event contours
+            see <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section10"/>
+
+      FAhA  spatial direction
+            see <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section28"/>
+
+      VA    spatial distance
+            vi = short, va = medium, vu = long
+
+      VEhA  spatial interval
+            ve'i = short, ve'a = medium, ve'u = long, ve'e = infinite
+
+      VIhA  spatial dimensionality
+            vi'i = line, vi'a = plane, vi'u = space, vi'e = space-time
+
+      FEhE  spatial interval modifier flag
+            fe'enoroi = nowhere, fe'eroroi = everywhere, fe'eba'o = beyond, etc.
+
+      MOhI  spatial movement flag
+            mo'i = motion; see <xref linkend="cll_chapter10-section28"/>
+
+      KI    set or reset sticky tense
+            tense+“ki” = set, “ki” alone = reset
+
+      CUhE  tense question, reference point
+            cu'e = asks for a tense or aspect, nau = use speaker’s reference point
+
+      JAI   tense conversion
+            jaica = the time of, jaivi = the place of, etc.
+</programlisting>
+</section>
+
+<section xml:id="cll_chapter10-section28">
+  <title>28. List of spatial directions and direction-like relations</title>
+  <para>The following list of FAhA cmavo gives rough English glosses for the cmavo, first when used without “mo'i” to express a direction, and then when used with “mo'i” to express movement in the direction. When possible, the gismu from which the cmavo is derived is also listed.</para>
+  <programlisting>
+cmavo   gismu   without mo'i        with mo'i
+-----   -----   ------------        ---------
+ca'u    crane   in front (of)       forward
+ti'a    trixe   behind              backward
+zu'a    zunle   on the left (of)    leftward
+ri'u    pritu   on the right (of)   rightward
+ga'u    gapru   above               upward(ly)
+ni'a    cnita   below               downward(ly)
+ne'i    nenri   within              into
+ru'u    sruri   surrounding         orbiting
+pa'o    pagre   transfixing         passing through
+ne'a            next to             moving while next to
+te'e            bordering           moving along the border (of)
+re'o            adjacent (to)       along
+fa'a    farna   towards             arriving at
+to'o            away from           departing from
+zo'i            inward (from)       approaching
+ze'o            outward (from)      receding from
+zo'a            tangential (to)     passing (by)
+bu'u            coincident (with)   moving to coincide with
+be'a    berti   north (of)          northward(ly)
+ne'u    snanu   south (of)          southward(ly)
+du'a    stuna   east (of)           eastward(ly)
+vu'a            west (of)           westward(ly)
+</programlisting>
+  <para>Special note on “fa'a”, “to'o”, “zo'i”, and “ze'o”:</para>
+  <para>“zo'i” and “ze'o” refer to direction towards or away from the speaker’s location, or whatever the origin is.</para>
+  <para>“fa'a” and “to'o” refer to direction towards or away from some other point.</para>
+</section>
+
